extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of constitutional law and political science; educated readers and policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for analyzing and designing the executive branch and its relation to legislatures and subnational units, with comparative examples (United States vs France) and attention to institutional safeguards and practical circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrain_state_independence
rubrics_metrics.description: The object of the federal constitution was not to destroy the independence of the states, but to restrain it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By acknowledging the real authority of these secondary communities, the constitution disavows the habitual use of constraint in enforcing majority decisions; the introduction of state influence into the federal mechanism is to be expected and should be accommodated rather than forcibly checked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different_principles_of_representation_senate_vs_house
rubrics_metrics.description: The Senate named by the provincial Legislature — the Representatives, by the People.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differences include mode of election (Senate elected by an elected body; House directly by the people), terms (Representatives two years; Senators six), and functions (House purely legislative and impeaching body; Senate cooperates in legislation, tries impeachments, ratifies treaties, and confirms appointments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive_elective_and_responsible
rubrics_metrics.description: The president is an elective magistrate; he is elective and responsible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: His honor, property, liberty, and life are securities for temperate use of power. He is subject to inspection (not direction) by the Senate; salary fixed at entry to office; provided with a suspensive veto to oppose laws that might destroy his constitutional independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive_need_for_stability_and_strength
rubrics_metrics.description: The executive power must enjoy a greater degree of stability and of strength than had been granted to it in the separate states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The president is chosen for four years and may be re-elected so that prolonged administration can enable long-term public undertakings; but care is taken not to render his decisions subordinate to a council which would clog action and diminish responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative_encroachment_and_mitigations
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislative assemblies can encroach upon executive independence (e.g., by depriving an officer of salary); constitutions should provide mitigations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fixing the president's salary for the term and granting a suspensive veto are measures that reduce legislative leverage; nevertheless, dependence of the executive on the legislature is a defect inherent in republican constitutions and must be managed rather than eliminated.

rubrics_metrics.name: President_as_executor_not_co-legislator
rubrics_metrics.description: The President is the mere executor of the law and does not co-operate in its formation as a constitutional king might.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike a king who may appoint members of a chamber, dissolve another, or be represented in assemblies by ministers, the president cannot dissolve or directly shape the legislature and is excluded from congress; his influence penetrates only indirectly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration_and_durability_of_executive_authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Duration (hereditary or long tenure) is a chief element of executive strength; the president's shorter, elective term weakens authority relative to a hereditary monarch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Durability makes authority loved or feared; a president elected for four years lacks the durability of a hereditary king, which affects his practical influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability_vs_inviolability
rubrics_metrics.description: The president is responsible for his actions; the person of a monarch may be declared inviolable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political accountability constrains executive action in republics; inviolability in monarchies alters the balance of responsibility and protections for the executive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circumstantial_factors_affect_executive_influence
rubrics_metrics.description: External security, military/naval strength, and the nation's foreign relations needs increase the importance and practical power of the executive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even with formal prerogatives, lack of external threats, small armies, or few ships limit the opportunities for the president to exercise great prerogatives; conversely, dangerous circumstances increase executive activity and influence irrespective of formal constitutional powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dangers_of_elective_system_scale_with_prerogative
rubrics_metrics.description: Dangers of the elective system increase in proportion to the extent of the prerogative vested in the executive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an elected chief has broad privileges, election becomes a tempting prize for private ambition and can inflame factionalism; to make a powerful sovereign elective requires circumscribing its powers and conditioning the people to live without its protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions_favourable_for_an_elective_executive
rubrics_metrics.description: An elective executive is feasible where geography, laws, habits, manners, and opinions of the people admit of a weak and dependent executive government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A legislator must inquire into these circumstances before adopting an elective chief; favorable conditions (e.g., isolation, absence of powerful neighbors) mitigate dangers inherent to election.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electoral_cycle_effects_on_government_stability
rubrics_metrics.description: Elections introduce instability: government action is often suspended before elections and a change in executive can cause widespread turnover among public officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At the approach of an election the head is occupied by the struggle and suspends new initiatives; in elective systems many public offices turn over at each election, producing administrative discontinuity greater than in constitutional monarchies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Veto_as_suspensive_appeal_and_check
rubrics_metrics.description: The suspensive veto forces the legislature to reconsider measures and, if persisted in, requires a supermajority (two-thirds) to override; it is a sort of appeal to the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The veto is a security for the executive against secret oppression and a procedural tool to make the legislature deliberate further rather than an absolute barrier to lawmaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mode_of_election_and_safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: Skillful modes of election (e.g., creating a special electoral body, separate votes of electors, House chosen when no majority) can obviate difficulties inherent in mass or martial election methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design of the electoral mechanism should avoid exposing the polity to civil conflict (as when people meet in arms to choose a leader) and can introduce institutional filters (electoral colleges, contingency rules) to stabilize the process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unsettled_removal_powers_and_practical_implications
rubrics_metrics.description: The precise power of the president to remove executive officers without Senate sanction is unsettled and has been debated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambiguities over removal affect the executive's ability to choose and rely on agents; historical practice and legislative decisions have influenced but not definitively settled the matter, so constitutional design should acknowledge procedural uncertainty and its administrative consequences.
